newsitem.title: GERMANY: D.Telekom chief declines comment on C&W.
newsitem.headline: D.Telekom chief declines comment on C&W.

text.p: Telecommunications group Deutsche Telekom AG on Wednesday declined to comment on widespread speculation its Global One partnership could form ties to Cable and Wireless Plc.

Cable and Wireless is believed to be on the verge of leaving its German alliance with utility Veba AG and industry analysts have suggested it was seeking to join Telekom's alliance with France Telecom and Sprint Corp.
A senior Veba official said earlier this week that the company had made a "fair offer" to Cable and Wireless to buy the 45 percent stake it holds in their joint venture, Vebacom.

"We enjoy watching how these alliances in Germany change. But it was never the policy of Deutsche Telekom to discuss possible scenarios. I cannot say anything more than that," Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told reporters in Munich.

Asked if he recently met Cable and Wireless chief executive Richard Brown, Sommer said: "You know the answer to that. In this business everyone talks to each other, but that doesn't mean I'm going to outline my schedule for you."

Industry analysts have suggested that Global One, the international telecommunications alliance offering worldwide communications services for companies, would benefit from C&W's holdings in Hongkong Telecom.
Sommer said that for a long time the group had thought it needed one strong partner in Asia, but now this had changed.

"We have invested a lot in Asia. We know now that we cannot have just one Asian partner, but that we have to be present in a lot of countries," he said. "Besides, we feel very comfortable in Global One as a threesome, but that does not mean that we have shut the door forever."
Sommer said Deutsche Telekom had three main markets: Europe, Asia and the United States.
"Germany is our core market, but Europe is our home market," he said.
Commenting on the company's European expansion goals, he said Britain, Spain and Italy were the "three most important target markets."

Sommer was pleased with developments at Global One, which began offering services last year after a long regulatory battle with Brussels and Washington over the investment by France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom in Sprint.
Global One's main competitor is the Concert alliance between British Telecom and MCI, which plan to merge.
"If you compare us on an apples to apples basis, then Global One is about twice as big as Concert," he said. But he could not say if this was in terms of comparable revenue.
He said Global One currently had 30,000 customers worldwide. It made revenues of $800 million last year from February to December and expects up to $1.3 billion for all of 1997.
